props.title: The Naked Kiss

sections.content: Samuel Fuller's **The Naked Kiss** (1964) explodes onto screen with one of cinema's most shocking openings - a bald prostitute beating her pimp with a handbag. This sets the tone for a noir that defies every convention of its era. Like Fuller's earlier **Shock Corridor** (1963), it peels back small-town America's respectable veneer to expose festering corruption. The film's protagonist Kelly (Constance Towers) attempts to remake herself as a children's nurse, echoing similar themes of reinvention and redemption found in Douglas Sirk's **All That Heaven Allows** (1955), but with Fuller's characteristic brutality.

sections.content: Fuller's unflinching exploration of taboo subjects was revolutionary for 1964. While other films of the era like **Touch of Evil** (1958) dealt with corruption, **The Naked Kiss** ventures into territory few would dare - pedophilia, prostitution, and small-town hypocrisy. The film's stark black-and-white photography by Stanley Cortez (who also shot **The Night of the Hunter** (1955)) creates a world of harsh contrasts that mirror its moral landscape.

The influence of **The Naked Kiss** echoes through later maverick filmmakers. Martin Scorsese's **Taxi Driver** (1976) shares its themes of urban decay and redemptive violence, while David Lynch's **Blue Velvet** (1986) similarly explores the darkness lurking beneath suburban facades. Fuller's aggressive style and willingness to confront controversial subjects paved the way for the New Hollywood movement of the late 1960s and 1970s. SUBHEAD: Fuller's Visual Innovation

sections.content: Fuller's documentary background influences his raw visual style in **The Naked Kiss**. His use of handheld cameras and extreme close-ups creates an immediacy that would later influence directors like John Cassavetes in **Faces** (1968) and Robert Altman in **The Long Goodbye** (1973). The film's famous opening sequence, shot from the pimp's POV as he's beaten, demonstrates Fuller's ability to make violence both visceral and subjective.
